highlights.title: Sony and UMG are suing Suno again
highlights.summary: Sony and Universal Music Group filed yet another suit against Suno. The labels claim its new v6 model still infringes on their copyrights because it's trained on user outputs from previous models, which were themselves trained on unlicensed music ripped from YouTube and other sources.
body: “Training a ‘new’ model on the outputs of an infringing model does not eliminate the infringement; it launders it, passing the value of Plaintiffs’ expression from the copied recordings into the tainted models, from those models into their outputs, and from those outputs into v6 … V6 is not a fresh start; it is the fruit of the same poisoned tree.”

When v6 launched, Suno’s Jack Brody told The Verge it was “trained from the ground up, with a new set of data,” including “user data,” but did not offer details beyond that. Suno later confirmed to Engadget that data includes “creations” from users, but would not elaborate further when reached for comment.
Sony further alleges that Suno used distillation to train v6. It claims that it was trained to replicate the results of its previous, “teacher” models, which were created using infringing data.

The complaint says that “even a model not directly trained on Plaintiffs’ recordings is informed by, and benefits from, Suno’s retained unauthorized copies.” Essentially, the labels argue that, unless Suno truly starts from scratch, its models will continue to be built on stolen data.

highlights.title: 'They changed the plan' - Hamilton left frustrated by Ferrari tactics
highlights.summary: Lewis Hamilton expressed frustration with Ferrari's approach to Q3 after qualifying sixth for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, saying "they changed the plan".
body: Hamilton questioned why the team completed only one run of multiple laps at the end of the final knockout stage rather than go out earlier for initial laps, as Mercedes, McLaren and Red Bull with Max Verstappen had done.

The seven-time world champion said his final laps were compromised by having no 'tow' from a car in front to aid straight-line speed down Baku's long main straight. Team-mate Charles Leclerc did have a tow, from Hamilton, by dint of the fact it was the Monegasque's turn to go out second in final qualifying.
Leclerc qualified second behind dominant Mercedes polesitter George Russell, who topped qualifying by a season-high margin of eight tenths of a second.
Reflecting on his own session, Hamilton told Sky Sports F1: "It was a pretty bad qualifying once again. It's not for the lack of trying.

highlights.title: Microsoft thinks its new Copilot ‘super app’ will be as influential as Office
highlights.summary: After teasing its new Copilot "super app" last month, Microsoft is officially unveiling it today. The redesigned Copilot app bundles three AI capabilities into a single interface of chat, coding, and agents.
body: This new Copilot app will have three tabs for Home, Code, and Autopilot, with Home combining Copilot Chat and Cowork together. It’s the default landing experience for Copilot users, and Microsoft is also planning to include a Today feature inside it that works as a personalized dashboard for important emails, meeting requests, Teams threads, and more.

“Home is where you get your bearings, keeping you grounded and moving forward: review recent activity, get suggestions on what Copilot can help with, and pick up work right where you left off,” explains Jared Spataro, chief marketing officer of AI at work at Microsoft.

The Code tab is the surprise addition to this so-called “super app,” and not one you’d typically associate with an app designed for knowledge workers. It will let anyone create an app, tracker, dashboard, or automation and share the results with colleagues as cloud-hosted internal apps. “Powered by the same underlying technology as GitHub Copilot, Code runs in a sandboxed environment and can be hosted securely within your tenant,” says Spataro.

highlights.title: Brandon Sanderson’s New Cosmere Book Gets Exclusive New Reveal
highlights.summary: Brandon Sanderson 's adult fantasy books are set in the sprawling Cosmere universe, where godlike beings fight for power on planets with their own complex rules for magic. The Mistborn series takes place in the world of Scadrial while The Stormlight Archive is set on Roshar.
body: The sheer number of interconnected books Sanderson has written can make getting into the Cosmere feel intimidating, but he’s created a solution in the Hoid’s Travails series. That began with the releases of Tress of the Emerald Sea and Yumi and the Nightmare Painter in 2023, the standalone books can be read in any order. The only connection to the vast Cosmere is Hoid, the storytelling trickster who appears in most of Sanderson’s works.

The next book in the series, The Fires of December, releases digitally on Oct. 6 and physically on Dec. 6. It was part of a BackerKit campaign last year for a Hoid’s Storybook Collection that raised $11 million. It’s the only Cosmere book the exceptionally prolific author is releasing this year as he focuses on the Mistborn film adaptation, co-writing the modern fantasy book Songs of the Dead, and continuing his YA sci-fi Cytoverse series with Blightfall.

highlights.title: One company is at the center of a wave of rogue AI attacks
highlights.summary: In July, OpenAI revealed that its AI agents had attacked Hugging Face without permission, sparking widespread concerns about AI safety. Since then, a string of similar incidents involving agents from Meta, Anthropic, Google, and other companies has fueled further fears about rogue AI.
body: Mistakes at Israeli startup Irregular sent Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, and Google agents after real-world targets.

Irregular, an Israeli startup that stress-tests AI models in “high-fidelity research platforms that simulate and monitor real-world AI security scenarios,” has worked with many of the industry’s biggest players since it was founded as Pattern Labs in 2023. Its exact client list is not known, but its work has been cited in OpenAI model system cards, it was used to test systems for the UK government and Anthropic, and it published research with RAND, a highly influential think tank that informs policy on AI.
In several Irregular tests this year, agents escaped their supposedly secure testing environments and went after real-world targets.

The breaches, which are independent of the Hugging Face hack, all follow the same broad template: Irregular was testing the models’ cybersecurity capabilities in controlled environments meant to simulate realistic conditions. Some of the tests used “capture-the-flag” exercises, a common way of testing hacking abilities that asks agents to find hidden information inside of a simulated network. At least, the network is meant to be simulated.

highlights.title: Anthropic’s founders seek voting control ahead of IPO
highlights.summary: Anthropic is asking its shareholders to approve a structure that would give its seven co-founders a combined 50.1% of the vote on most corporate matters.
body: Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE.
This isn’t a new idea; super-voting shares are how Mark Zuckerberg kept control of Meta, and how Evan Spiegel maintained his hold of Snap. The list is long. What’s unusual is the group approach.

Why do it? The seven co-founders reportedly own just 2% of the company apiece, Amodei included, and have pledged to give away 80% of their wealth, a commitment the CEO announced in January alongside a warning that AI-driven wealth concentration could destabilize society. The new shares carry no extra economic value, but they’d preserve the group’s control once the company starts trading publicly.

There are twists, too: Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust would still choose most of the board; the founders’ board seats would grow from two to three; and employees would get their own stock to break ties on some issues.

highlights.title: After seven years, a spacecraft company is releasing its Otters into the wild
highlights.summary: Imagine starting a space company in October 2019 with the aim of changing the world. Then, a few months later, a global pandemic shuts the world down. "Little did we know what the world had in store for us," said Trevor Bennett, an engineer who co-founded Starfish Space after a few years at Blue…
body: At Blue Origin, he saw, up close, the ambitions of billionaires to build big rockets and put massive numbers of satellites into orbit. Bennett and his co-founder, another engineer from Blue Origin named Austin Link, began to think about the implications. How would humanity deal with that increased volume of satellites in orbit? Could low-Earth orbit be preserved?

Ideas like asteroid mining or building infrastructure on the Moon seemed a little too far out at the time, but improving the ability to move around in space, deorbiting threats, and extending the life of assets there seemed more plausible. An obvious business case was extending the life of large satellites in geostationary orbit, but just as important, Bennet and Link felt like managing these ever-growing constellations in low-Earth orbit would become vital.
“So we had two business cases that we thought were meaningful,” Bennett said. “What we needed was a vehicle to go match that, and that was Otter.”

highlights.title: The Pentagon wants $30 million to build an AI-powered lie detector
highlights.summary: The US government wants to spend $30.3 million over the next five years on an improved form of lie detector, according to a Department of Defense budget request. The program, called Polygraph+ or Polygraph Next, will focus on scoring algorithms that use artificial intelligence and machine learning…
body: According to details of the budget document, which were first reported by Inside Defense, the project will “modernize federal polygraph and credibility assessment technologies” to improve their accuracy and reliability. But the project may be just the latest in a long line of failed attempts to use technology to detect lies. “It’s a misguided effort to reduce the complex to something that is tangible,” says Kyri Kotsoglou, a legal scholar at Northumbria University in the UK who studies the use of polygraphs in the justice system.

The move comes at a time of high tension within the department. Under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has been increasingly turning to polygraph tests in an attempt to find the sources of alleged leaks to the press. In September, the New York Times reported that around 50 officers on the Joint Staff had been given polygraph tests after news coverage reported on the depletion of US weapons stockpiles in the war with Iran.

body: Insider Gaming reported that Ubisoft Milan, co-developer of the Mario + Rabbids games, once pitched Nintendo on "an original Zelda spinoff starring a previously unknown protagonist." It called the project Goliath, "a name that reflected the scale of what Ubisoft Milan aimed to develop." Nintendo gave it the initial greenlight, but wanted Ubisoft to make Ganondorf the player character instead. The villainous Ganondorf is as essential to The Legend of Zelda series as Link and Zelda are, but is only playable in spinoff games like Hyrule Warriors and in the Super Smash Bros. games.

Ubisoft Milan worked throughout the year on a prototype, but Nintendo rejected that prototype in November. "The reasons for [Nintendo's] decision remain unclear," Insider Gaming said. It's also not clear what that prototype looked like or what type of game it would have been.

highlights.title: Pokémon 30th Anniversary Jirachi Card Price Explodes After Tragic Death
highlights.summary: For people who buy and sell Pokémon cards, the period right after a set releases is a chaotic one. Prices for illustration cards move in unpredictable ways, but the trend is almost always downward.
body: The reason is a sad one. Earlier in September, news broke that 12-year-old Pokémon influencer Avery The Poke Kid passed away after a prolonged fight against cancer. Avery's cheerful attitude, despite his trying circumstances, made him a beloved figure in the Pokémon community. Avery often featured in content where he encouraged people to cherish the cards they had, regardless of value. He also reminded people about the importance of living life to the fullest — and he did so in between chemotherapy sessions and surgeries.

Prior to passing away on Sept. 18, Avery's parents recorded a final video of him opening one more Pokémon pack. Much to his delight, the last pack he ever opened contained the Jirachi ex #155 card, illustrated by Akira Egawa. The bittersweet pack opening went viral, in part due to the significance of the card Avery pulled.

highlights.title: ‘Charlie Harper’ Review: Emilia Jones and Nick Robinson Come Apart, in Fits and Starts, in a Fuzzy, Non-Linear Breakup Drama
highlights.summary: The first thing to know about “Charlie Harper” is that it’s not, in fact, about someone called Charlie Harper. Charlie (Nick Robinson) and Harper (Emilia Jones) are a couple, meeting and parting at various stages across a five-year timeline; the title of this earnestly melancholy first feature by…
body: The stars are appealing enough in Mac Eldridge and Tom Dean's directorial debut, but can't quite make us care about the ill-starred couple they play.

We begin, naturally, somewhere in the middle: Our introduction to the principals is not theirs to each other. When Charlie approaches Harper in a low-lit bar to introduce himself, she says they’ve met before, jogging his memory about their first encounter way back in high school. But this is just another round of a game they’ve played before, with the shoe on the other foot, and when we circle back to that same scene toward the close, we’re more conscious of the weight of what has transpired between them. Starting over as strangers would be sweeter and easier.

highlights.title: US being left behind in EV charging speeds as China goes sub-5 min to 70%
highlights.summary: Hype merchants have a habit of overdoing it, but there’s no denying that China is making the US look more than a little antiquated when it comes to electric vehicles. Some of that is due to a deep integration of connected services and an extension of the car as part of the owner’s digital…
body: China might have a much younger driving culture than North America or Europe, but it has still been long enough to condition those drivers to how long it takes to fill a tank of gas. For all their many improvements over internal combustion engine vehicles—far greater efficiency, instant torque, very little NVH, more reliabiity, and so on—EVs do still take longer to recharge than it takes to refuel a car with a liquid.

Geely’s new battery can charge at up to 2.2 MW and will recharge from 10 to 70 percent in 4.5 minutes. A 10–98 percent charge takes 8 minutes 40 seconds. Predictive thermal management is done through AI, with an average pack temperature of 55˚C and a peak temperature during charging of 65˚C, Geely said.

And while you might think pumping large amounts of energy into a battery quickly and repeatedly could harm its health, Geely says that, using AI, the system applies micro pulses of current to “reactivate lithium ions accumulated at the negative electrodes during repeated fast charging,” extending battery life by 20 percent. The pack has been tested in both the Zeekr 001 and Lynk and Co 10—maybe we’ll see a Volvo or Lotus use the same tech someday.

highlights.title: Game, set … match? Can a dating coach help you win at love?
highlights.summary: Would you pay thousands to meet the love of your life? In an age of app fatigue, many singles are hiring coaches to help them find partners. But are they chancers preying on the lovelorn, or do they hold the key to true romance? Modern dating is a hellscape.
body: Modern dating is a hellscape. Just ask any single person, who will probably regale you with stories of endless swiping, ghosting, cringe Hinge dates and unfulfilling “situationships”. But what if there was a way to escape all this and put yourself on a fast track to finding The One?

How did the coaching actually work? Yarrow’s programme was based around identifying Izzy’s “limiting beliefs” about herself – for example, that she was “going to be single for ever” – and challenging the ways they were holding her back from finding love. The first step was delving into her romantic past, all the way back to her first kiss, to find the origin of her insecurities. “Through that, so many things surfaced – some of the terrible, awful horror stories I hadn’t really shared or picked up on, even from being a teenager,” Izzy remembers. “Obviously, that shapes who we are now. So we did a full retrospective.”

highlights.title: How One Crash Bandicoot Level Helped Build Naughty Dog
highlights.summary: From a quick-fix solution to a triple-A staple, this is how an early Crash Bandicoot level inspired decades of cinematic level design in Uncharted and beyond.
body: As Leon Kennedy, we fled from a giant, mechanical statue. Eleven years later, we guided Nathan Drake and his brother, Sam, as they escaped from relentless pursuers on a motorbike. And recently, we helped forge a path through a literal wave of plague-infested rats for A Plague Tale’s Amicia. Three examples from literally hundreds of cinematic chase sequences in video games that can all trace their roots back to an unlikely source. The colourful cartoon platformer that started it all: Crash Bandicoot.

The running-towards-camera chase sequence is as popular now as it’s ever been, raising the cinematic tension in blockbuster games for the last 30 years. But its beginnings were humble, and its widespread use is all thanks to the Crash developers at Naughty Dog trying to solve a single problem: How do we show our character’s face more?

“It’s the modern Naughty Dog playing the antique Naughty Dog.” said Jason Rubin, a co-creator of Crash Bandicoot, in a 2019 interview with IGN. “What Nathan’s doesn’t understand is that this is basically the game that led to you. You exist because of this game!”

highlights.title: Steal My Food Itinerary: 3 Days in Sifnos, Greece
highlights.summary: It felt like everyone I know traveled to Greece this summer. Friends chose Zakynthos, Crete, Naxos, Ikaria. I opted for Sifnos, one of the Cyclades’ most celebrated food destinations but still, thankfully, relatively under the radar internationally.
body: Just 3 hours from Athens by ferry, this Cycladic island is best experienced around the table.

Our trip landed in the middle of August — peak tourist season in the Mediterranean — but it never felt cramped. And now that summer has come to a close, what crowds there were have thinned and temperatures are more forgiving, yet peak-season produce is still finding its way into dishes across the island. So now is an even better time to experience Sifnos.

Getting there means starting in Athens, where ferries come in and out of the port of Piraeus from all across the Aegean and Ionian seas. The 2.5-hour trip from Athens to Sifnos is a thrill — worthy of a few Dramamine tablets if you’re prone to seasickness — with incredible views of the islands you pass along the way. The Aegean really is a different shade of blue; it’s tempting to gaze into it from the deck the whole way.
